# Try with Resources

This example shows why resource management is part of secure coding, not just
a style preference.

Leaked file descriptors, JDBC statements, result sets, and connections are
availability problems. In long-running services they can accumulate silently
and eventually turn into outages, stalled requests, or hard-to-diagnose
operational failures.

Java's try-with-resources feature exists to make resource lifetime explicit and
reliable. The examples in this project compare a manual `finally`-based
cleanup approach with a safer try-with-resources approach for both files and
JDBC resources.

## What you will learn

By the end of this example you will understand:

- why resource leaks are an availability and therefore a security concern
- how manual cleanup with `finally` is more error-prone than scoped automatic
  cleanup
- why try-with-resources reduces the time a resource stays open
- how try-with-resources closes dependent JDBC resources in reverse order
- why an example can still be unsafe even when it does not fail immediately on
  your machine

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 21 or newer](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java21)

This example uses the Maven Wrapper (`./mvnw`), so you do not need to install
Maven separately.

## Inspect the manual-cleanup file example

Start with the vulnerable-style implementation in `App.java`.

The code opens a large number of temporary files and keeps every
`FileOutputStream` in a list until the very end of the method, where a `finally`
block attempts to close them all.

What you gain from this step: you see the exact lifetime problem. The code does
eventually close resources, but it keeps all of them open far longer than
necessary.

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.resources;

import java.io.File;
import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public final class App {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<FileOutputStream> openFiles = new ArrayList<>();
        int fileCount = 0;

        try {
            for (fileCount = 1; fileCount <= 20_000; ++fileCount) {
                // Create a temporary file
                File tempFile = File.createTempFile("demo", ".tmp");

                // Open a FileOutputStream to the file without closing it
                FileOutputStream fos = new FileOutputStream(tempFile);
                openFiles.add(fos);

                if (fileCount % 1000 == 0) {
                    System.out.println("Opened file: " + fileCount);
                }
            }
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.err.println("IOException caught: " + e.getMessage());
            System.err.println("Number of files opened before exhaustion: " + fileCount);
            e.printStackTrace(System.err);
        } finally {
            // Attempt to close all opened file streams (important for real applications)
            for (FileOutputStream fos : openFiles) {
                try {
                    fos.close();
                } catch (IOException e) {
                    System.err.println("Error closing file: " + e.getMessage());
                }
            }
            System.out.println("All opened file streams closed in the finally block.");
        }
    }
}
```

This is the subtle point many teams miss: "eventually closed" is not the same as
"safely scoped". If the method opens thousands of resources before cleanup runs,
the process can still exhaust file descriptors or create operational pressure
long before `finally` gets a chance to help.

On some systems this program will eventually fail with an error such as
`Too many open files`. On others, like the run shown above, it may finish all
iterations successfully.

That difference is environmental, not conceptual. The exact failure point
depends on the operating system and the per-process file descriptor limit. The
core problem is still the same: all those file descriptors remain open until
the `finally` block runs.

This is why the example belongs in a secure-coding workshop. Availability bugs
often hide until runtime pressure makes them visible.

## Inspect the try-with-resources file example

Now look at the remediated version.

The fixed variant still creates the same number of files, but the
`FileOutputStream` is scoped to a try-with-resources block inside the loop, so
each stream is closed immediately after that iteration completes.

What you gain from this step: you see that the important improvement is not
"different cleanup code" but a different resource lifetime.

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.resources;

import java.io.File;
import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.IOException;

public final class App_fixed {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int fileCount = 0;

        try {
            for (fileCount = 1; fileCount <= 20_000; ++fileCount) {
                // File itself is not Closeable. The resource we must release is the
                // FileOutputStream created for it.
                File tempFile = File.createTempFile("demo", ".tmp");
                try (FileOutputStream fos = new FileOutputStream(tempFile)) {
                    // The stream is closed automatically at the end of this block.
                    fos.write(new byte[0]);
                }

                if (fileCount % 1000 == 0) {
                    System.out.println("Opened file: " + fileCount);
                }
            }
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.err.println("IOException caught: " + e.getMessage());
            System.err.println("Number of files opened before exhaustion: " + fileCount);
        }
        System.out.println("All file streams were closed automatically by try-with-resources.");
    }
}
```

The visible progress output is intentionally similar. That is part of the
lesson.

The safer code does not necessarily produce a dramatic new functional result.
The improvement is in the resource lifetime and the failure surface:

- each `FileOutputStream` is closed at the end of its iteration
- the code no longer relies on one large cleanup pass at method exit
- the leak window is much smaller
- the cleanup logic is easier to audit

## Inspect the JDBC example

The JDBC example is the stronger live demonstration because it shows close
ordering directly.

Here one resource depends on another: the `ResultSet` depends on the
`Statement`, and the `Statement` depends on the `Connection`. The code opens
them in order inside a single try-with-resources statement.

What you gain from this step: you see how try-with-resources handles multiple
dependent resources safely and predictably.

```java
package com.oracle.jsc.resources;

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;

import org.flywaydb.core.Flyway;

import com.oracle.jsc.resources.jdbc.MyDriverManager;

public final class FunWithJDBC {
    private static final String URL = "jdbc:h2:file:./test";
    private static final String USER = "sa";
    private static final String PASS = "";

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("~~~ setting up the database ~~~");
        Flyway flyway = Flyway.configure().dataSource(URL, USER, PASS).load();
        flyway.migrate();

        System.out.println("\n~~~ retrieving some data ~~~");
        try (Connection connection = MyDriverManager.getConnection(URL, USER, PASS);
                Statement statement = connection.createStatement();
                ResultSet resultSet = statement.executeQuery("SELECT * FROM catalogue_item")) {

            while (resultSet.next()) {
                // Assuming 'id' is an integer column and 'name' is a string column
                int id = resultSet.getInt("id");
                String name = resultSet.getString("caption");
                System.out.println("ID: " + id + ", Name: " + name);
            }

            System.out.println("\n~~~ cleaning up ~~~");
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            e.printStackTrace(System.err);
        }

        System.out.println("\n~~~ Done! ~~~");
    }

}
```

The example uses small wrapper classes around JDBC types so `close()` calls are
printed to the console. Those wrappers are there purely to make the closure
order visible during the workshop.

Running this example also creates or updates local H2 database files in the
example directory, such as `test.mv.db`.

## Run the JDBC example

Run the JDBC example now.

What you gain from this step: a deterministic demonstration that resources are
closed in reverse order of acquisition.

```shell
java --class-path 'target/try_with_resources-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar' com.oracle.jsc.resources.FunWithJDBC
```

Observed output

```
...
~~~ retrieving some data ~~~
ID: 1, Name: Leather Sofa
ID: 2, Name: Wooden Table
ID: 3, Name: Plastic Chair
ID: 4, Name: Mug
ID: 5, Name: LED TV

~~~ cleaning up ~~~
Closing ResultSet.
Closing Statement.
Closing Connection.

~~~ Done! ~~~
...
```

The close order matters:

- `ResultSet` closes first
- then `Statement`
- then `Connection`

That reverse ordering is exactly what you want for dependent resources. It is
harder to get right consistently with manual cleanup, especially once code paths
and exception handling become more complex.

## What this example teaches

- Resource management is part of secure coding because leaked resources can
  become availability failures.
- A `finally` block is better than no cleanup, but it still encourages
  longer-lived resources and more complex error handling.
- Try-with-resources makes the lifetime of a resource local, explicit, and
  easier to review.
- With multiple resources, try-with-resources closes them in reverse order
  automatically.
- The absence of immediate failure on your machine does not prove the code is
  safe.
